extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (general readers interested in Locke's theory of ideas)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating clarity and adequacy of ideas
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and judge whether an idea is distinct or confused, real or fantastical, and adequate or inadequate according to Locke's criteria; includes guidance on causes of confusion and how complex ideas (modes, relations, substances) should be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confused idea (mutable idea assigned to multiple names)
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea that, being changeable or not fixed to one precise combination of simple ideas, is used under different names (e.g. CHURCH or IDOLATRY) and so 'loses the distinction' that distinct names are designed for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an idea is called confused because a mutable idea cannot belong to one name rather than another. The remedy is to attend to steady, precise combinations of simple ideas under a single name so distinctions are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion presupposes comparison with another idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion always concerns two ideas — difficulty in separating two things that should be separated involves an idea that approaches another and risks being confounded with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When suspecting confusion, examine which other idea it is in danger of being confounded with (same as, a part of, or as justifiably called by that other name). Identify the other idea (usually one denoted by a different name) to reveal the lack of sufficient distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of confused ideas (loose application of names and complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion often arises from the loose application of names to undetermined, variable, or almost no ideas; also from ideas being so complex that memory cannot retain the precise combination of simple ideas under one name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevention: collect and unite into one complex idea, as precisely as possible, all ingredients whereby it is differentiated from others, and apply the same name steadily. Anti-patterns: accommodating ease or vanity, using names loosely to cover ignorance or to perplex others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial clarity in complex ideas (distinct in one part, confused in another)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex idea may be clear and distinct in one component and obscure in another, leading to error when one assumes the whole idea is distinct based on familiarity with only one part (example: chiliaedron — clear idea of the number thousand but confused idea of the figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of reasoning that stays only on the clear part of a composite idea; testing by varying the unclear part (e.g. altering figure while keeping number) will reveal the confusion. Do not draw confident deductions about the obscure part from the familiar part of the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite concepts cause confused ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of actual infinities (e.g., Eternity, infinite divisibility of matter) are confused because we cannot form a clear, complete idea of the whole extent; we only have relative, obscure notions that something is 'bigger' beyond any finite comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning about infinites (eternity, infinite divisibility) is liable to blunders and manifest absurdities due to the obscurity. Recognize that our clear ideas pertain only to finite aspects (e.g., number) and not to the actual infinite parts; avoid asserting positive, determinate properties about the infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real ideas (criteria: foundation in nature / conformity with archetypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real ideas have a foundation in nature and a conformity with the real being and existence of things (their archetypes); they represent the powers in things that produce sensations in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple ideas (effects of powers in things) are all real because they are constantly produced by those powers. For an idea to be real it suffices that it corresponds steadily to constitutions of real beings (whether as causes or patterns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastical (chimerical) ideas (no foundation in nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantastical or chimerical ideas have no foundation in nature and no conformity with the reality to which they are tacitly referred as archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex ideas of substances that join simple ideas never actually found united in any substance (or that contain inconsistency) are fantastical (examples: a rational creature with a horse's head joined to a human body, or contradictory mixtures of properties). Assess whether the combination is possible or known to exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed modes and relations are real if possible/consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed modes and relations (complex ideas made by the mind) are real so long as they consist of consistent ideas and there is a possibility of existing conformably to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mixed modes are archetypes created by the mind rather than copies of external patterns, they are adequate to themselves if coherent. They may be deemed improper or fantastical only relative to common linguistic signification (misnaming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of substances are real only when they agree with existing things
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas of substances (which aim to represent substances as they really are) are real only insofar as their combinations of simple ideas actually co-exist in things without us; otherwise they are fantastical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a substance-idea by whether its constituent simple ideas correspond to a real, observed unity in nature. If the collection has never been found united, treat it as imaginary; if it contains contradictions, it is certainly chimerical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate ideas (perfect representation of archetypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate ideas are those that perfectly represent the archetypes they are intended to stand for; inadequate ideas are partial or incomplete representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple ideas are all adequate because they are produced by the powers of things and correspond to them. When assessing adequacy ask whether the idea contains everything required to represent its archetype fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes (complex ideas made by the mind) are generally adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas of modes (mind-made combinations) are inherently adequate because they are intended to be patterns created by the mind and so contain everything the mind intended them to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mode is adequate as an internal standard, but can become inadequate insofar as an individual intends it to correspond exactly to another person's idea (i.e., when a mode is used with reference to a settled name and another's pattern). In that case, measure adequacy by correspondence to the other person's archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances are inadequate when referred to unknown real essences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of substances are inadequate if they are meant to represent supposed real essences of species, because people lack ideas of those essences and thus their substance-ideas cannot be full representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If names of substances are taken to stand for unknown 'real essences', then the ideas tied to those names are necessarily inadequate. Ask whether the idea purports to capture an unknown internal constitution; if so, treat it as deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances as collections of qualities are inadequate (practical reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when ideas of substances are formed by collecting observable qualities and powers, they remain inadequate because no one complex idea contains all the many and various simple ideas (powers) that a substance actually has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the complex idea includes all known and potential powers of the substance — it almost certainly does not. Example: the common idea of GOLD (colour, weight, hardness, fusibility) omits innumerable other properties; therefore substance-ideas based on limited qualities are partial and insufficient for a true essence.
